meta.title: Who really said "There are years that ask questions and years that answer"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes—this one is real. Zora Neale Hurston wrote it as the opening line of Chapter 3 of her 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are years that ask questions and years that answer'?
meta.ogDescription: A genuine Hurston line: it opens Chapter 3 of Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), confirmed by Quote Investigator and Wikiquote.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1891–1960 · American novelist, anthropologist & folklorist of the Harlem Renaissance
answer.sourceLine: It is the opening line of Chapter 3 of Hurston’s 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God: “There are years that ask questions and years that answer. Janie had had no chance to know things, so she had to ask.” Quote Investigator traces it to that original publication and finds no earlier source.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: There are years that ask questions and years that answer. Janie had had no chance to know things, so she had to ask. Did marriage end the cosmic loneliness of the unmated? Did marriage compel love like the sun the day?
trail: Quote Investigator concludes Hurston “deserves credit” and traces the wording to the 1937 first edition, Chapter 3.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) section, citing Ch. 3.
The line is one of the novel’s most quoted; it circulates widely on Goodreads and quotation sites, all crediting Hurston’s 1937 novel.
source.excerptNote: The line opens Chapter 3, as Janie’s first marriage fails to bring the love she expected. Page numbers vary by edition (Quote Investigator cites p. 38; Wikiquote cites p. 21).

author.name: Zora Neale Hurston
author.heading: About Zora Neale Hurston
author.bio: Zora Neale Hurston was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance and a trained anthropologist who collected African American and Caribbean folklore. Her best-known novel, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), traces Janie Crawford’s search for selfhood and voice through three marriages in the rural South. Long out of print at her death in poverty, Hurston’s work was revived in the 1970s—championed by Alice Walker—and is now firmly in the American literary canon.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: In the novel, the line arrives as Janie’s idealized first marriage collapses into disappointment—a moment when experience, not instruction, becomes her teacher. Hurston frames whole seasons of a life as either questioning or answering, a rhythm readers recognize far beyond the book.
Lifted out of context, it reads as gentle life-wisdom, which is why it thrives on inspirational feeds. But unlike most such lines, this one is genuinely traceable to a real, dated, authored work.
